newsitem.title: USA: Justice Department clears Bell-Nynex merger.
newsitem.headline: Justice Department clears Bell-Nynex merger.

text.p: The Justice Department announced unconditional approval of Bell Atlantic Corp.'s $20 billion stock merger with Nynex Corp. Thursday, clearing the way for creation of the nation's second-largest phone company.

"The (Justice Department antitrust) division has decided that it will not challenge the transaction, having concluded that the merger does not violate the antitrust laws," the department said in a one-paragraph press release, one year and two days after the deal was announced.
The new Bell Atlantic, headquartered in New York, would rank second only to AT&T Corp., serving the eastern seaboard from Maine to Virginia, including 13 states and the District of Columbia.
"We're extremely pleased with the Department of Justice's decision," Ray Smith, Bell Atlantic's chairman and chief executive, said in a statement.
Although the Federal Communications Commission must sign off on the deal, it has traditionally followed the Justice Department's lead in such matters.

The new Bell Atlantic will be gargantuan by any corporate measure. It will rank 23rd on Fortune magazine's list of the 500 largest U.S. corporations, gross about $30 billion a year, operate 37 million phone lines in the United States and another 3 million abroad, and provide service to 5 million wireless phone customers.

The merger shrinks the number of regional Baby Bell phone companies -- created by break-up of AT&T in 1984 -- from seven to five. Earlier this month, San Antonio, Texas-based SBC Communications Inc. completed its $16.5 billion purchase of Pacific Telesis Group.
Like the SBC-PacTel deal, the Bell Atlantic-Nynex marriage is a product of last year's comprehensive telecommunications act, which spawned a free-for-all in the communications business.
The law tore down 62-year-old legal barriers and allows local and long-distance phone companies, cable-television operators and others to invade each other's turf.
Smith said in his statement the new company is ready to compete vigorously across the board.
"Our merger will continue to open communications markets -- local, long-distance and video -- and help realise the promise of the 1996 Telecom Act," he said.
Nynex Chairman Ivan Seidenberg, exulting in a similar vein, promised the merger would "promote customer choice, innovation and economic growth in the communities we serve."

But analysts suggested the government took a darker view privately. They noted the telecommunications law is aimed at creating a new, fiercely competitive business environment in which poorly positioned companies face the risk of perishing.

"While many in Justice for policy reasons feared this merger, legally they couldn't block it," said analyst Scott Cleland of Schwab Washington Research Group. "They didn't have the evidence of an antitrust violation."

The merger decision was made by Joel Klein, acting chief of the Justice Department's antitrust division. It was announced only five days before Klein faces a Senate confirmation hearing to become permanent chief. He is expected to win confirmation from the full Senate.
Klein said in a speech last month he favoured any merger that achieves efficiencies, "so long as this consolidation doesn't erode competitive opportunities in any market."
At the same time, Klein made it clear that he was looking beyond America's borders in considering the competitive potential of companies.
"The United States is positioned for global competition in a way that is the envy of the world," he said of American communications companies.
